attribution.note: Zitron's own sentence in his own post, which he endorses.

semantics.note: A firm present-tense observation, faithfully normalised. The concession about scientific and analytics uses that follows is kept in the contract.

contract.note: Reading 'very little else' as meaning practical, economic usefulness outside AI is ordinary. Excluding isolated scientific examples respects his concession. The May 2026 window was picked by the evaluator, but it is reasonable for an ongoing state.

evidence.note: A preprint showing GPU acceleration of FP64 finite-element work on GH200/GB200. These are scientific uses the speaker already allowed, and it gives no share of capacity or workload inventory for AI facilities.
A provider blog from August 2026, after the target month. It describes non-AI GPU workloads and says AI-oriented hardware may fit them poorly. No workload shares or economics.

reviews.rationale: Neither item measures how much non-AI work AI-oriented GPU facilities actually run, or what it is worth. e1 shows scientific uses the speaker conceded. e2 is later, and if anything leans toward the hardware fitting non-AI work poorly. Nothing settles 'very little else' for May 2026.

attribution.note: Zitron's own sentence in his own post.

semantics.note: Revision 2 correctly restores 'don't appear to be' and 'heavily-suggests'. Both premise and conclusion are hedged inferences, not firm assertions.

contract.note: The contract scores the claim on a plain reading even though both clauses are hedged ('don't appear', 'heavily-suggests'). Policy allows plain-reading scoring only for firm language. The three generations, the cost metric and the test for 'broken' are all supplied by the evaluator.

evidence.note: An independent February 2026 benchmark, with ownership-cost estimates, finding much better tokens per dollar on Blackwell than Hopper. It cuts against the no-reduction premise, but the hedged claim is not scored.

reviews.rationale: The statement is hedged: costs 'don't appear' to be falling, which 'heavily-suggests' a broken model. Under the policy, graded or tentative language is not scored. e1 is strong benchmark evidence against the premise and is recorded, but it cannot score a hedged inference.

attribution.note: Zitron's own sentence in his own post.

semantics.note: A compound claim: a past observation about Blackwell plus a firm, open-ended forecast about Rubin. 'It' refers to AI. The normalisation keeps both parts and states no deadline.

contract.note: Reading 'cheaper' as unit cost for comparable work is an ordinary reading, although the speaker's wider point concerns total costs as models grow. The early-resolution rule, which requires a documented deployed-cost reduction, is fair.

evidence.note: NVIDIA's own blog reporting a lower benchmark cost per million tokens for GB200 than H200. It is a manufacturer disclosure about its own product, not an independent finding, so it does not settle the Blackwell part on its own.

A CoreWeave release from September 2026 reporting Cognition's throughput gains and 'lower cost per session'. It gives no prices or quality-controlled cost figures, so it does not meet the early-resolution rule.
NVIDIA's September 2026 claim of up to 45x lower Rubin token cost on benchmarks. A manufacturer disclosure, not a documented deployed-workload cost.

reviews.rationale: The Rubin forecast has no deadline, and no item documents a comparable reduction in deployed cost, so it cannot be scored yet. The Blackwell part is challenged only by NVIDIA's own disclosure, and this case's packet has no independent measurement. Overall unresolved.

attribution.note: Zitron's own sentence in his own post.

semantics.note: The normalisation drops the 'companies paying actual costs are screaming for mercy' element. It also turns 'unaffordable for most', which sits inside a 'could be a theoretical future' clause, into a flat assertion. 'Built on subsidized subscriptions' is a causal claim about demand, matching the contract's causal axis.

contract.note: The contract covers all three elements and reads 'mirage' as subsidy-dependent demand, which is an ordinary reading. Thresholds such as 'more than half' and the Q1 2026 window were chosen by the evaluator, but they are reasonable.

evidence.note: A Stanford survey from March 2026 measuring users' willingness to accept compensation for giving up AI. It shows users value the tools, but it does not measure ability to pay full-cost prices.

An NBER paper, available before the evaluation date, using April 2026 card data: about 2.9% of US consumers pay, mostly for plans of $30 or less. It is outside the target quarter and has no provider cost data.

reviews.rationale: No item ties provider full costs to customer affordability or retention, or shows what happens to demand when subsidies are removed. e1 and e2 are context on how users value AI and how they pay. Whether subsidies cause demand, and whether customers face full-cost pressure, cannot be settled from this packet.
